Cluster 01 DRILL: Viral Structure and the Phage Cycles

H2 Biology 9477 · Book 4 · 8 questions · 76 marks · 31 parts · one mark per minute, so a little over an hour and a quarter · every question is an actual exam paper question

Answers sit directly under each part, hidden. Click Show answer only after you have said your full reasoning aloud for that part. Check (a) before you start (b), that is the point of the layout.

Rate your confidence before every reveal. A dashed line sits above each answer block. Say high, medium or guessed out loud before you click. A right answer said hesitantly stays ACTIVE; a right answer said confidently moves on.

Every question below is a real exam paper question. The stem is the paper's own wording, and the paper, year and question number are named in the Sources block at the foot of every question. Where a stem has been edited it is only so that it stands without the parts of the original that came before it, and the edit is written out in that same block. If a question cannot be traced to a paper, it is not in here.

Eight questions, 76 marks, 31 parts. The set is sized for coverage, not for the clock. Questions 1 to 4 are viral structure, the viral genome and the cell theory, 36 marks; questions 5 to 8 are the phage cycles, 40 marks. Two sittings is a reasonable way to run it.

The anchors. Question 4(a) is 9477 Specimen Paper 1 Question 3 word for word, the only official Cambridge item that exists on this cluster. Question 5(b) is SAJC's 2023 Paper 3 Section B essay at its real 10 marks, and it is the full-cycle question: the lytic cycle end to end, five stages, no shortcuts.

Six real figures, five questions figure-led. Book 4 runs at 43.8% figure-led overall and 45.7% among structured parts, higher than any Book so far, so nearly half of every structured question here opens with a diagram or a micrograph. Every figure is the real image from the paper the question came from, not a redrawing. Two further figures could not be recovered from their papers; those parts carry the paper's own description as prose instead, and say so.

No read-off-the-graph parts. The two graphs in this drill are stimulus for an explain question and nothing else. Question 6(b)'s graph carries no numbers at all, so the marks are for the induction mechanism, not for the trend.

Two MCQs, both real, both audited. The paper awards one mark for the letter. The drill then asks you to explain your answer, which is where every option has to be justified rather than three of them dismissed.

Cumulative over Books 1, 2 and 3. Q2(a) and Q2(c) need histones, linear chromosomes and chromosome number from Book 2. Q3(b), Q3(c) and Q3(d) need transcription, translation and DNA replication said cold. Q5(a) needs amino acids, peptide bonds and levels of protein structure from Book 1 held against nucleotides, phosphodiester bonds and the double helix from Book 2. A Book 1 or Book 2 gap surfacing here is worth more than a clean Cluster 1 answer, so say it out loud when it happens.

What the marks reward. Write capsid, not protein coat, on a labelling part. Write viral envelope, not phospholipid bilayer and not protein envelope. Keep the bilayer host-derived and the glycoproteins virally encoded, because a scheme prints a reject for saying both came from the previous host. Say template and synthesis, never conversion. Give every comparison point to point on the same feature. On any phage answer, the capsid is left outside the bacterial cell wall, and water enters by osmosis after lysozyme digests it.

One primary concept each, checked for duplicated required ANSWERS and not just for duplicated labels. Q1 reading an unfamiliar enveloped virus and saying where each part came from · Q2 three viruses that are on no syllabus, described on the axes the outcome names · Q3 what the genome type forces the virion to carry · Q4 the cell theory tested statement by statement · Q5 the lytic cycle end to end, plus protein against nucleic acid as molecules · Q6 why a phage would ever choose not to kill its host · Q7 phage anatomy mapped to function, and what happens when the receptor does not fit · Q8 the lytic cycle turned into a therapy, and where the therapy fails. The one shared idea in the set is that viruses are acellular, which Q4(b) needs alongside the crystallisation and ATP arguments and Q4(c) needs alongside the host-resources argument; the two parts are marked on different points and neither answer is the other. Every other pair was checked at the level of the paragraph the scheme demands, and no two questions need the same one.

Nothing from Books 5 to 9, and nothing from Clusters 2 or 3 of this Book. The influenza and HIV reproductive cycles, antigenic shift and drift, and the whole of bacterial genetics are later clusters, so no question here needs them. Where influenza appears it is only as a genome to compare against, at the level of eight negative-sense segments. Vaccines, antibodies and immunity are Extension Topic A and are out of scope in every answer.

Question 1 [9 marks]

Fig. 1.1 shows the structure of a coronavirus, SARS-CoV, which caused the Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome (SARS). Infection by SARS-CoV causes symptoms resembling influenza that can be deadly.

(a) Identify structures A to D. [2]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (a)

(a) Fig. 1.1, identify structures A to D. [2]

1. Any two correct identifications earn one mark, so four correct identifications earn both marks.

2. A is the viral envelope. Reject "protein envelope" and "phospholipid bilayer".

3. B is RNA.

4. C is nucleoproteins, accept RNA-binding proteins. Reject "histone", "NS proteins", "replicase", "RNA-dependent RNA polymerase" and "antigen".

5. D is glycoprotein. Reject "HA", "NA", "proteins" and "antigen".

6. Examiner comment: "this question part is poorly done. The number of students who are unable to identify the parts or are misidentifying them is concerning. Students need to be more specific in their labelling of structures C and D instead of simply writing them as 'proteins'."

(b) State the origins of structures A and D. [1]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (b)

(b) State the origins of structures A and D. [1]

1. Structure A is from the previous host cell and structure D is from the virus.

2. Accept structure A as phospholipids and membrane proteins from the previous host.

3. Reject: both came from the previous host cell.

4. Examiner comment: "this part of the question was not well attempted; the majority of students simply wrote that both A and D came from the previous host. Students need to realise that glycoproteins are necessary for viruses to infect host cells, hence they must be produced from the viral genome."

(c) With reference to Fig. 1.1, compare the structures of SARS-CoV-2 and influenza virus. [3]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (c)

(c) With reference to Fig. 1.1, compare the structures of SARS-CoV-2 and influenza virus. [3]

1. Similarity: both are enveloped, that is both have a viral envelope.

2. Similarity: both are enclosed or encapsulated by nucleoprotein, that is both have a nucleocapsid.

3. Similarity: both have glycoproteins.

4. Similarity: both have RNA.

5. Difference: influenza virus has eight single-stranded viral RNA segments but SARS-CoV-2 has one single-stranded viral RNA.

6. Difference: influenza virus has segmented viral RNA but SARS-CoV-2 has non-segmented viral RNA.

(d) Describe the structural components of virus. [3]

---

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (d)

(d) Describe the structural components of virus. [3]

1. Viral genome contains either DNA or RNA, that can be single or double stranded.

2. Genome can be circular or linear, and there can be more than one copy of the genome.

3. All viruses have capsid protein that either surrounds the nucleic acid or encloses it.

4. The capsid is made from identical protein subunits known as capsomeres.

5. The capsid protects the viral genome and determines the specific shape of the virus.

6. Viral envelopes are phospholipid bilayer membrane derived from the host cell membrane.

7. The envelope is embedded with glycoprotein and surrounds the capsid.

8. Glycoproteins are essential for the attachment of virus to host cell receptor.

9. The envelope protects the virus from enzymes, chemicals and a harsh environment.

Sources & concepts

Source: School (HCI) Prelim 2024 P2 Q4(a), stem, Fig. 4.1 and key with all rejects and the examiner comment verbatim (a); School (HCI) Prelim 2024 P2 Q4(b), stem, key and examiner comment verbatim (b); JPJC Prelim 2021 P2 Q5(a), reprinted as HCI Topical 2021 STQ Q7(a), stem and key verbatim (c), with the figure reference renumbered from Fig. 5.1 to Fig. 1.1 so the part stands on this question's own figure; MI Prelim 2018 P2 Q2(a), stem and key verbatim (d). The figure is the real Fig. 4.1 from the HCI 2024 Paper 2 question paper. Archetype: structure identification off an unfamiliar virus diagram, then origin of each structure, then a point-to-point comparison, then a cold description. Data and figure interpretation is the single largest archetype in this Book at 32.3% of in-scope records, and viral structure is the single largest node at 41.0%. Trap: writing "protein coat" or "phospholipid bilayer" where capsid and viral envelope are the wanted words; saying both the envelope and its glycoproteins came from the previous host, which the scheme rejects by name; giving the comparison as a list of what SARS-CoV-2 has rather than as matched pairs on the same feature; forgetting that the genome axis in (d) has four separate parts, DNA or RNA, single or double stranded, circular or linear, and copy number. LOs: 1(e) structural components of viruses including enveloped viruses, and interpreting drawings of them, in (a), (b), (c) and (d); 2(d) the structure and organisation of viral genomes in (c) and (d). Concepts fused: (1) envelope identification; (2) genome identification from a drawn thread; (3) nucleoprotein against capsomere; (4) glycoprotein as a distinct label from protein; (5) host-derived bilayer; (6) virally encoded glycoproteins; (7) segmented against non-segmented genome; (8) capsid built from identical capsomeres; (9) capsid function as protection and shape; (10) glycoprotein function in attachment; (11) envelope function in protection.

Question 2 [9 marks]

The human papillomavirus (HPV) is sexually transmitted and can cause the development of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN). Patients with CIN are observed to have abnormal growth of cells that line the cervix. This can lead to the development of cervical cancer. Fig. 2.1 shows the structure of the HPV.

(a) With reference to Fig. 2.1, compare the structure of HPV with a T4 bacteriophage. [3]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (a)

(a) With reference to Fig. 2.1, compare the structure of HPV with a T4 bacteriophage. [3]

1. Similarity: the genome of both viruses is enclosed by a protein capsid, or both viruses have a capsid which is made up of several individual protein subunits, that is capsomeres.

2. Similarity: both viral genomes are made up of DNA.

3. Difference: the HPV has DNA associated with histone protein, while the T4 bacteriophage DNA does not associate with histone protein.

4. Difference: spherical capsid against icosahedral capsid head.

5. Difference: T4 bacteriophage has a sheath, collar, tail and tail fibres, name any one, while the HPV does not. Accept, only if neither of the two previous points is given, that the HPV has a spherical shape while the T4 bacteriophage has a complex shape.

6. Difference: the HPV has 2 types of capsid proteins, L1 and L2, while the T4 bacteriophage has only 1 type.

(b) Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) is an enveloped virus whose genome is double-stranded DNA. List two differences between the EBV and influenza virus genomes. [2]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (b)

(b) List two differences between the EBV and influenza virus genomes. [2]

1. DNA against RNA.

2. Double-stranded against single-stranded.

3. One molecule, that is non-segmented, against eight molecules, that is segmented.

4. The command word is list, so two one-line statements, each stated for both viruses.

(c) Hantaviruses are a group of viruses that normally infect rodents, but do not cause disease in them. Humans may become infected with Hantaviruses through contact with rodent urine, saliva, or faeces. The genome of the virus consists of three segments, small, medium and large. With reference to Fig. 2.2, describe three structural features which distinguish the Hantavirus from its human host cell. [3]

Figure not recovered. Described from the source paper: Fig. 2.2, a roughly spherical enveloped virion. The lipid envelope carries the G1 and G2 surface glycoprotein spikes. Inside are three separate circular ribonucleoprotein segments, small, medium and large, each an RNA molecule coated with nucleocapsid protein, together with molecules of RNA-dependent RNA polymerase.
Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (c)

(c) With reference to Fig. 2.2, describe three structural features which distinguish the Hantavirus from its human host cell. [3]

1. Genome. Hantavirus genome is made up of ribonucleotides, that is RNA, whereas the human host cell genome is made up of deoxyribonucleotides, that is DNA.

2. Enzyme for genome replication. Hantavirus has RNA-dependent RNA polymerase for viral RNA genome replication whereas the host uses DNA polymerase for DNA replication. Alternatively, on the enzyme for mRNA synthesis, Hantavirus has RNA-dependent RNA polymerase for viral mRNA synthesis whereas the host uses DNA-dependent RNA polymerase for transcription.

3. Structure of the genome. Hantavirus RNA segments are circular, that is joined at the ends, whereas host chromosomes are linear.

4. Genome organisation. Hantavirus RNA genome consists of three segments whereas the host genome is made up of 46 chromosomes.

5. Proteins bound to the genome. Hantavirus has nucleocapsid protein bound to the viral RNA genome whereas the host has histone proteins bound to the human DNA genome.

6. Any other valid point is credited.

(d) Human cytomegalovirus (HCMV) is a common enveloped virus affecting humans. Structure T, the shell built from many hexagonal facets that encloses the viral DNA, is always the same shape. However, electron micrographs show that HCMV virions are not all the same shape. Suggest why HCMV virions can appear in different shapes. [1]

---

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (d)

(d) Suggest why HCMV virions can appear in different shapes. [1]

1. There is the presence of a viral envelope made up of phospholipid bilayer, therefore fluid or flexible, resulting in different shapes.

2. Alternatively, there is reference to preparation for electron microscopy that results in distortion, a squashed sample or an artefact.

3. An additional valid point is a suggestion of variation in the number, arrangement or organisation of tegument protein.

Sources & concepts

Source: RI Prelim 2024 P3 Q1(a), stem, Fig. 1.1 and key verbatim (a); NJC Prelim 2024 P2 Q4(a)(ii), stem and key verbatim (b), with the EBV genome description folded into the stem from the paper's own Fig. 4.1 caption so the part stands alone; EJC Prelim 2021 P2 Q5(a)(i), stem and key verbatim (c), with the paper's Fig. 5.1 renumbered 2.2 and its description carried in the stem because the image could not be recovered; SAJC Prelim 2024 P3 Q2(b), stem and key verbatim (d), with structure T described inline in place of the paper's Fig. 2.1B. The Fig. 2.1 image is the real Fig. 1.1 from the RI 2024 Paper 3 question paper. Archetype: predict and apply to a novel case. Three of the four viruses here, HPV, Hantavirus and HCMV, appear in no syllabus and none is on the school's list. Apply-to-novel-case is 14.1% of the in-scope Book 4 corpus against Book 3's 1.7%, which is the single sharpest difference between the two Books. Trap: giving one-sided differences instead of point-to-point pairs; forgetting that a virus can carry histones only if it takes them from the host; treating "three segments" as the only Hantavirus point when the enzyme, the circularity and the bound protein are each separate marks; describing HPV as a naked virus without saying what the T4 has instead. LOs: 1(e) structural components of viruses including bacteriophages, and interpreting drawings of them, in (a) and (d); 2(d) the structure and organisation of viral genomes and, by contrast, eukaryotic genomes, in (a), (b) and (c). Reach-back to Book 2 genome organisation for histones, linearity and chromosome number in (c). Concepts fused: (1) capsid as the shared feature of naked and tailed viruses; (2) capsomere subunit structure; (3) histone association as a borrowed eukaryotic feature; (4) capsid symmetry; (5) phage-specific structures; (6) number of capsid protein types; (7) DNA against RNA genome; (8) strandedness; (9) segmentation; (10) which polymerase a genome type forces the virion to carry; (11) circular against linear genome; (12) nucleocapsid protein against histone; (13) envelope fluidity as the cause of pleomorphism.

Question 3 [9 marks]

(a) The Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) infects human host cells of multiple organ systems, resulting in the disease COVID-19. Its genome is single-stranded RNA of positive sense, about 30 kb in length. Both influenza virus and SARS-CoV-2 replicate their own genome. The influenza virus carries its own viral RNA polymerase in its virions but not SARS-CoV-2. Suggest why. [2]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (a)

(a) The influenza virus carries its own viral RNA polymerase in its virions but not SARS-CoV-2. Suggest why. [2]

1. The influenza virus genome is negative sense RNA, and there is no available enzyme in host cells to use negative sense RNA as a template to make positive sense RNA.

2. Whereas SARS-CoV-2 has a positive sense RNA genome, which can be used directly as a template for translation using host ribosomes to make the viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase.

3. So the point is not that a host RNA-dependent RNA polymerase exists for one virus and not the other. Neither virus has one available. The difference is that a positive-sense genome can make its own polymerase after entry, and a negative-sense genome cannot be read at all until a polymerase it brought with it has copied it.

(b) Rubella virus contains a single positive sense RNA strand as the genetic material. Suggest how the positive sense RNA strand of rubella virus is utilised in making progeny virus. [2]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (b)

(b) Suggest how the positive sense RNA strand of rubella virus is utilised in making progeny virus. [2]

1. Viral polymerase converts positive sense RNA to negative sense RNA to use as a template for synthesis of more copies of positive sense RNA.

2. Positive sense RNA is the template for translation of viral proteins.

3. Marker's note: unlike influenza, rubella has a positive sense RNA genome, so it can directly be used for translation; reverse transcriptase is not involved.

(c) RNA-dependent RNA polymerase can be found in the influenza virion while reverse transcriptase can be found in retroviruses. Besides the type of virus, describe one similarity and two differences between RNA-dependent RNA polymerase and reverse transcriptase. [3]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (c)

(c) Describe one similarity and two differences between RNA-dependent RNA polymerase and reverse transcriptase. [3]

1. Similarity: both are viral proteins, that is they are only coded for by viral genes and not the host genes.

2. Similarity: both are dependent on RNA as a template.

3. Difference in template used: RNA-dependent RNA polymerase uses RNA, both positive and negative strand, whereas reverse transcriptase uses an RNA template first and then the single-stranded cDNA.

4. Difference in products: RNA-dependent RNA polymerase only forms RNA, that is positive-sense RNA for translation when using negative RNA as a template, and negative RNA when using positive RNA as a template to create more copies of the viral genome, giving single-stranded RNA; reverse transcriptase forms a cDNA-RNA hybrid using RNA as template, then double-stranded cDNA when using cDNA as a template.

5. Difference in catalytic activity: RNA-dependent RNA polymerase has RNA polymerase activity, that is extension of RNA using host free ribonucleotides, whereas reverse transcriptase has reverse transcription activity, that is extension of cDNA, ribonuclease or RNase activity, that is degrading RNA in the cDNA-RNA hybrid, and DNA polymerase activity, that is formation of complementary DNA to form double-stranded cDNA.

6. Difference in monomers: ribonucleotides against deoxyribonucleotides.

(d) The Central Dogma describes the flow of genetic information from DNA to RNA to proteins. Explain, with an example, how the Central Dogma may not always hold true. [2]

---

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (d)

(d) Explain, with an example, how the Central Dogma may not always hold true. [2]

1. There can be reverse flow of genetic information from RNA to DNA. For example, in HIV, reverse transcriptase produces DNA from viral RNA, that is reverse transcription occurs in HIV.

2. RNA instead of DNA can store genetic information. For example, the influenza virus has several segments of linear negative single-stranded RNA genome.

3. RNA can undergo replication. For example, influenza virus contains RNA-dependent RNA polymerase which synthesises positive-sense RNA using negative-sense RNA as the template via complementary base pairing.

4. Any one point plus its example earns one mark, and two such pairs earn both marks.

Sources & concepts

Source: SAJC Prelim 2025 P2 Q4(a)(ii), stem and key verbatim (a), with the paper's Fig. 4.1 genome caption folded into the stem so the part stands without the figure; School (HCI) Prelim 2023 P3 Q2(b), stem, key and marker's note verbatim (b); PJC Prelim 2017 P2 Q5(b), stem and key verbatim (c), with "this virion" replaced by "the influenza virion" so the part stands alone; MJC Prelim 2013 P2 Q2(a), stem and key verbatim (d), with the paper's Fig. 2.1 flow chart described in the stem in one clause. Archetype: mechanism explain-chain, 12.5% of the in-scope Book. Every part here is a why, and every mark is a link in a chain rather than a recalled fact. Trap: saying that RNA is converted or turned into DNA, or that negative sense RNA is converted into positive sense, both of which a scheme rejects by name, when the language wanted is template and synthesis with the original strand surviving; claiming the host has an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase for one virus and not the other; giving reverse transcriptase only one activity when the scheme credits three; naming an example in (d) without stating which principle of the central dogma it breaks. LOs: 2(d) the structure and organisation of viral genomes, specifically DNA against RNA and sense, in (a), (b) and (d); 1(e) the viral enzymes carried in the virion in (a) and (c). Reach-back to Book 2 for transcription, translation and DNA replication throughout (d). Concepts fused: (1) positive sense as directly translatable; (2) negative sense as needing a template step first; (3) why the virion has to carry an enzyme it cannot make yet; (4) the same positive-sense strand serving twice, as mRNA and as template; (5) the naming convention for a dependent polymerase; (6) RNase H activity; (7) the DNA polymerase activity that finishes the second cDNA strand; (8) ribonucleotides against deoxyribonucleotides; (9) reverse information flow; (10) RNA as a hereditary molecule; (11) RNA replication with no DNA stage.

Question 4 [9 marks]

(a) Which features of viruses provide evidence that they are non-living? [1]

1 Viral nucleic acids can be cut into small fragments by bacterial restriction enzymes. 2 Complete virus particles usually contain only one type of nucleic acid. 3 Virus particles can be isolated and crystallised. 4 Viruses cannot synthesise ATP.

A1, 2 and 3
B1, 2 and 4
C2, 3 and 4
D3 and 4 only
Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (a)

(a) Which features of viruses provide evidence that they are non-living? [1] [INFERRED: the 9477 specimen papers ship without a mark scheme; cross-checked against YIJC Prelim 2025 P1 Q16, which sets the same content with six numbered statements and whose key audits each one]

1. The key is C, features 2, 3 and 4.

(b) Explain your answer, stating for each of the four numbered features whether it is evidence that viruses are non-living, and why. [3]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (b)

(b) Explain your answer, stating for each of the four numbered features whether it is evidence. [3] [INFERRED: reasoning taken from the YIJC Prelim 2025 P1 Q16 key, which audits the same statements]

1. Feature 1 is not evidence. Being cut by bacterial restriction enzymes is about the susceptibility of DNA and RNA, not about whether the virus is alive, and DNA and RNA from living organisms can equally be cut by restriction enzymes.

2. Feature 2 is evidence. Every living cell contains both DNA and RNA, whereas a virion carries only one type of nucleic acid, so it lacks the full genetic information needed for independent life.

3. Feature 3 is evidence. A virus can be crystallised like a pure chemical, which no living cell can.

4. Feature 4 is evidence. Viruses have no metabolism of their own and cannot generate ATP, so they must use the host cell's energy supply.

5. Note for the related YIJC version of this question: lacking cellular structure alone does not directly explain obligate parasitism; the key is the absence of metabolic and energy-generating systems.

(c) Ebola is a rare yet deadly infectious disease. The virus that causes Ebola is known as the Ebola virus (EBOV). EBOV is an enveloped virus containing a cylindrical nucleocapsid that encloses an RNA genome and a viral enzyme. Explain why viruses are considered obligate parasites. [2]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (c)

(c) Explain why viruses are considered obligate parasites. [2]

1. Viruses are acellular, that is they lack cellular or biosynthetic machinery or organelles required for survival or for metabolic reactions.

2. Viruses need to use the host cell's resources for synthesis of viral proteins and nucleic acids to complete the reproductive cycle.

3. The one-mark version of the same question is marked as requires a host cell in order to reproduce, or unable to reproduce outside of a host cell.

(d) Marseillevirus is a virus that infects amoeba. It is taken up by amoeba via phagocytosis. Upon membrane fusion, new progeny viruses are formed through DNA replication and protein synthesis. The progeny viruses are then released as the amoeba is lysed. Fig. 4.1 shows the structure of Marseillevirus. With reference to Fig. 4.1 and the information provided, explain how Marseillevirus challenges the cell theory. [3]

---

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (d)

(d) With reference to Fig. 4.1 and the information provided, explain how Marseillevirus challenges the cell theory. [3]

1. Identify why Marseillevirus is not considered as a cell, making reference to Fig. 4.1, for example that the figure shows only a capsid, an inner membrane and genomic DNA, with no ribosomes, no cytoplasm and no organelles.

2. Identify how Marseillevirus exhibits living characteristics with reference to the context, for example that it replicates its DNA and synthesises proteins to form new progeny viruses inside the amoeba.

3. Identify one tenet of the cell theory that it challenges, that is cells are the basic unit of life, or all living things are made from cells, or all cells come from pre-existing cells.

Sources & concepts

Source: 9477 Specimen Paper 1 Question 3 in full, verbatim from the official question paper (a); the follow-on wording in (b) is the drill's, and the reasoning is the YIJC Prelim 2025 P1 Q16 key verbatim, that paper setting the same four features among six with a full per-statement audit; YIJC Prelim 2023 P2 Q4(b)(iv), stem and key verbatim (c), with the EBOV preamble kept from the paper; VJC Prelim 2024 P2 Q1(b), stem, Fig. 1.2 and key verbatim (d), renumbered Fig. 4.1. The Fig. 4.1 image is the real Fig. 1.2 from the VJC 2024 Paper 2 question paper. Archetype: evaluate and discuss, only 1.4% of the in-scope corpus and almost all of it concentrated on this one node, plus the specimen's own MCQ, which is not plain recall but a test of each statement against a criterion of life. Trap: reading the restriction-enzyme statement as evidence because it sounds molecular; answering (d) with the non-living side only, when the scheme requires a living characteristic and a named tenet as well; answering (c) with "cannot reproduce outside a host" alone when the two-mark version wants the acellular point and the host-resources point; drifting into vaccines and immunity, which belong to Extension Topic A. LOs: 1(f) how viruses challenge the cell theory and concepts of what is considered living, in (a), (b), (c) and (d); 1(e) structural components, read off Fig. 4.1, in (d). Question 5 [12 marks]

(a) Fig. 5.1 shows a type of virus called a T2 phage. It consists of a protein coat enclosing a DNA molecule. This DNA causes the bacterial cell to make new copies of the T2 phage. State two ways in which the structure of the protein coat of T2 differs from the structure of its DNA. [2]

Figure not recovered. Described from the source paper: Fig. 5.1, a drawing of a T2 bacteriophage: a polyhedral head containing a coiled DNA molecule, a collar, a contractile tail sheath, a base plate and tail fibres.
Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (a)

(a) State two ways in which the structure of the protein coat of T2 differs from the structure of its DNA. [2]

1. The protein coat is built from amino acids, the DNA from deoxyribonucleotides, that is sugar plus phosphate plus base.

2. The protein coat uses peptide bonds, the DNA phosphodiester bonds.

3. The protein coat has secondary, tertiary and quaternary structure, the DNA is double stranded, that is a double helix.

4. The protein coat has 20 types of subunit, the DNA has 4 types of subunit, that is A, T, C and G.

5. Maximum two, each stated for both structures.

(b) Describe the reproductive cycles of bacteriophages that reproduce via a lytic cycle, such as the T4 phage. [10]

---

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (b)

(b) Describe the reproductive cycles of bacteriophages that reproduce via a lytic cycle, such as the T4 phage. [10]

1. Adsorption. Attachment sites on the phage tail fibres recognise and bind to complementary receptor sites on the bacterial cell wall.

2. Penetration. Lysozyme at the tip of the base plate degrades the bacterial cell wall and plasma membrane.

3. The tail sheath contracts and drives a hollow tube through the cell wall and membrane into the bacterium, injecting the genome into the bacterial cytoplasm.

4. Replication. Viral DNA is used as a template to make new viral DNA genome using the host DNA polymerase.

5. Viral DNA is transcribed to form viral mRNA using host RNA polymerase.

6. Viral mRNA is then translated to form viral proteins and enzymes using host ribosomes. Name any one use of those proteins: to shut down the host's macromolecular synthesis, that is protein, RNA and DNA synthesis; to hydrolyse the DNA of the host, recycling the nucleotides for the synthesis of new copies of phage DNA; or to direct the host's transcription and translation machinery, for example RNA polymerase and ribosomes, to synthesise phage enzymes and phage structural components for the assembly of new T4 phages.

7. Maturation. Viral proteins self-assemble to form the capsid head, tail and tail fibres of the new bacteriophages.

8. The phage genome is packaged inside the capsid head.

9. Lysozyme is packaged into the base plate.

10. Release. Phage-encoded lysozyme breaks down the bacterial peptidoglycan cell wall, causing lysis of the host cell and release of viral particles which spread to nearby cells and infect them.

11. Quality of written communication: obtain at least 1 mark each from a minimum of 3 out of the 5 stages of the reproductive cycle.

12. Two further marks routinely credited elsewhere in the corpus and worth adding: the capsid is left on the outside of the bacterial cell wall, and water enters the cell by osmosis, causing the cell to swell and burst, which is marked separately from the enzyme action.

Marking point 12 is added from the mark schemes attached to ACJC Prelim 2024 P2 Q5(b)(i) and the school's own chapter, and is flagged as an addition rather than part of the SAJC key. Book 4 essays are process-led: almost every one of the 22 essay-scale in-scope stems in the corpus asks for a process laid out in order and then for one thing to be said about it. This is the rehearsed process on which three of those essays depend. Trap: starting at penetration and skipping adsorption; saying the phage enters the cell rather than that the DNA is injected and the capsid stays outside; forgetting that host DNA is degraded and recycled as nucleotides, which is a mark in its own right; giving lysis as one mark when the enzyme action and the osmotic entry of water are marked separately; describing the protein coat and the DNA in (a) with only one of the two named, when every difference has to be stated for both. LOs: 2(e)i outlining the reproductive cycle of bacteriophages that reproduce via the lytic cycle, in (b); 1(e) structural components of bacteriophages in (a) and (b). Reach-back to Book 1 for amino acids, peptide bonds and levels of protein structure and to Book 2 for nucleotides, phosphodiester bonds and the double helix in (a). Question 6 [12 marks]

(a) Fig. 6.1 shows the reproductive cycles of a temperate bacteriophage, of which the lambda phage that infects Escherichia coli is an example. What is a lambda phage? [1]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (a)

(a) What is a lambda phage? [1]

1. It is a temperate phage as it is able to go through a lytic cycle and destroy the host cell or enter a lysogenic stage where the virus integrates into the bacteria's DNA as a prophage.

(b) Fig. 6.2 shows the changes in the number of extracellular lambda phages after they are introduced into a culture of E. coli. With reference to the reproductive cycle of temperate bacteriophages, explain why the number of phages increased after a brief UV irradiation. [3]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (b)

(b) With reference to the reproductive cycle of temperate bacteriophages, explain why the number of phages increased after a brief UV irradiation. [3]

1. UV triggers the switch from the lysogenic cycle to the lytic cycle, that is induction of the lytic cycle, causing the prophage to be excised from the host bacterial chromosome.

2. Enzymes in host cells, or host cell machinery, give at least two examples, replicate the viral DNA, and transcribe and translate the viral DNA into new viral components.

3. Lysis of host cells to release bacteriophages.

(c) Temperate phage replicates through both the lysogenic and lytic cycles. Suggest why it may be advantageous for a phage to have a lysogenic cycle. [4]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (c)

(c) Suggest why it may be advantageous for a phage to have a lysogenic cycle. [4]

1. Phage DNA or genome integrates itself into the host cell's chromosome, genome or DNA and becomes dormant as a prophage.

2. Phage DNA, genome or prophage can also be replicated each time the host cell or bacterium divides.

3. Hence a large number of viral particles can be assembled upon prophage induction.

4. This allows the phage to survive for long periods when conditions are unfavourable for viral reproduction, such as lack of nutrients or presence of harsh chemicals.

5. When conditions change, the prophage can switch back to the lytic cycle and start reproducing again.

(d) In addition to plasmid vectors, the insulin gene may be packaged into bacteriophage particles for delivery into E. coli. State whether a virulent or temperate phage would be used and explain how it could be engineered to deliver the insulin gene into bacteria. [4]

---

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (d)

(d) State whether a virulent or temperate phage would be used and explain how it could be engineered to deliver the insulin gene into bacteria. [4]

1. Temperate phage.

2. The phage carrying the human insulin gene attaches to specific receptors on the E. coli cell surface.

3. The phage penetrates the bacterial cell wall by contracting the contractile sheath of the tail, which drives the hollow tube of the tail into the host bacterium.

4. The human insulin gene packaged in the phage capsid is injected into the bacterial cytoplasm.

5. The human insulin gene can be integrated into the bacterial chromosome to enable expression of the insulin gene.

6. The phage will not cause the death of the host cell.

7. Bacteria reproduce asexually by binary fission and can be cultured in large quantities, leading to a high yield and a continuous, abundant supply of insulin.

Question 7 [6 marks]

(a) The diagram shows the structure of a T4 virus with its components labelled P to S. Which statement is not correct? [1]

AStructure P is made up of multiple subunits and serve to contain double stranded RNA.
BStructure Q is hollow and capable of contractile movement.
CStructure R has a specific conformation that is complementary to the bacterial cell wall.
DStructure S is where lysozyme is released to digest part of the bacterial cell wall.
Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (a)

(a) The diagram shows the structure of a T4 virus with its components labelled P to S. Which statement is not correct? [1]

1. The key is A.

(b) Explain your answer, saying why each of the other three statements is correct. [3]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (b)

(b) Explain your answer, saying why each of the other three statements is correct. [3] [INFERRED: the HCI Paper 1 mark scheme gives the letter only; reasoning cross-checked against VJC Prelim 2025 P1 Q11 and ASRJC Prelim 2022 P1 Q9, whose keys give the same structure-to-function mapping]

1. A is the incorrect statement. Structure P is the capsid head and it is made up of multiple identical protein subunits called capsomeres, which is correct, but it contains double-stranded linear DNA and not double-stranded RNA. T4 is a Group I double-stranded DNA virus.

2. B is correct. Structure Q is the contractile tail sheath. It is hollow, and conformational changes cause it to contract, driving the tail core through the bacterial cell wall and cell membrane.

3. C is correct. Structure R is a tail fibre. It carries attachment proteins whose conformation is complementary to specific receptor sites on the bacterial cell surface, which is what sets the host range of the phage.

4. D is correct. Structure S is at the base plate, and T4 uses lysozyme to hydrolyse peptidoglycan, degrading a portion of the bacterial cell wall so that the tail core can be inserted.

(c) A particular strain of E. coli bacteria was spread throughout the surface of a nutrient agar plate. Four solutions, each containing different lytic phages A, B, C and D, were then introduced into each quadrant of the agar. The plate was incubated for 24 hours to allow bacterial cells to divide and grow into a lawn. Areas where bacteria were absent showed up as clear zones. Clear zones were observed only in the quadrant where phage A was introduced but were not observed in the other three quadrants. Explain how infection by phage A resulted in clear zones. [2]

---

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (c)

(c) Explain how infection by phage A resulted in clear zones. [2]

1. Only phage A can bind to the bacterial cells due to its tail fibre being complementary in shape to the receptors on the bacterial cell surface, therefore it can infect.

2. Hence it can infect and cause osmotic lysis of the bacterial cell, which shows up as clear zones.

1. Lambda phage.

(c) A study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences revealed a plausible strategy to facilitate the replacement of antibiotic resistant pathogens with sensitive ones in hospitals. Researchers developed and administered two different phages that target the common gut microbe E. coli. The first was just a standard lytic phage that results in the death of the bacterial cell. Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (c)

(c) Explain how a lytic phage results in the death of the bacterial cell. [2]

1. Viral DNA genome codes for proteins, which do any one of the following: hydrolyse host DNA; shut down macromolecular synthesis, that is DNA, RNA and protein synthesis; or direct the host's transcription and translation machinery, for example RNA polymerase and ribosomes, to synthesise phage enzymes and phage structural components for the assembly of new phages.

2. Phage-encoded lysozyme lyses the bacterial cell to facilitate release of phages, thus killing the cell.

(d) To eradicate harmful bacteria, some scientists researched on developing a modified bacteriophage that could destroy the bacteria. Describe and explain how the reproductive cycle of such bacteriophages would be able to destroy the bacteria without harming humans. [4]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (d)

(d) Describe and explain how the reproductive cycle of such bacteriophages would be able to destroy the bacteria without harming humans. [4]

1. Modified T4 bacteriophages, or phages that undergo the lytic cycle, infect bacteria by binding to specific receptors on the cell surface.

2. The phage injects viral DNA into the host cell, and the viral DNA codes for enzymes that shut down metabolic activities of the host and degrade the host cell's DNA.

3. The phage replicates its genome and synthesises its proteins using the host cell's metabolic machinery, that is enzymes and ribosomes, and phage-coded lysozyme lyses the bacterial cell wall to release assembled phages from the bacterium to infect other bacteria.

4. Human cells do not have the receptors that allow attachment of phages.

(e) Suggest a limitation for using bacteriophages against bacteria causing tuberculosis. [1]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (e)

(e) Suggest a limitation for using bacteriophages against bacteria causing tuberculosis. [1]

1. Any one. M. tuberculosis bacteria are not easily accessed due to their presence inside host macrophages or cells.

2. There is the possibility of bacteria having a random mutation to change the shape of their receptors, so phage attachment sites cannot bind.

3. Mycobacteriophages are targeted by the human immune system and eliminated before they are able to affect the targeted bacteria.

4. The phage might undergo latency and outcomes are not immediate.

(f) "T4 bacteriophages are possible viral vectors to deliver correct genes to human immune cells." Discuss whether this statement is true and explain your reasoning. [1]

Say your confidence out loud before revealing: high / medium / guessed.
Answer - part (f)

(f) Discuss whether T4 bacteriophages are possible viral vectors to deliver correct genes to human immune cells. [1]

1. Bacteriophages are viruses that infect bacteria, so they lack the necessary proteins and mechanisms to enter human cells. Hence, they cannot directly deliver genes into human immune cells.

2. Examiner feedback: a significant number of students missed the point that viruses have specific hosts; having a lytic or lysogenic cycle has no impact in such an instance.
